metaTitle: Influencer Marketing: Tiers, Rates and Briefs
metaDescription: Influencer marketing is paying creators to reach their audience. The nano-to-mega tiers, typical Indian rate ranges, and how to brief so a campaign lands.
definition: Influencer marketing is paying a creator to promote something to the audience they've built, usually per post, per campaign, or on a monthly retainer.
answer: Influencer marketing is paying creators to put your product in front of the audience they've built. Tiers run from nano (1,000–10,000 followers) to mega (1 million plus), and rates move with them. A nano creator at ₹3,000–₹15,000 a post often out-converts a ₹5 lakh celebrity placement — trust doesn't scale with follower count.
takeaways: Four tiers: nano, micro, macro, mega. They're used for genuinely different jobs, not for different budgets.
**Reach is the wrong buying metric.** Cost per qualified enquiry is the right one, and it usually favours the small end.
Follower counts are trivially bought. Ask for a screen recording of insights, not a screenshot.
Disclosure isn't optional in India. ASCI's guidelines require an upfront, prominent label wherever there's a material connection.

sections.h2: The tiers, and what each one is actually for
body: Tier boundaries are conventions, not rules; agencies shift them by a few thousand followers. What matters is that each tier does a different job, and paying macro rates for work a micro creator does better is how this budget usually gets wasted.

callout.title: Read that table as ranges, not a rate card
callout.body: These are asks commonly quoted in the Indian market, not published prices, and they move hard. Category swings them most: a finance creator and a lifestyle creator with identical follower counts quote very different numbers. Exclusivity, usage rights and whitelisting each add to the base.

sections.h2: Why the smallest creators often convert best
body: A nano creator's audience is mostly people who know them — colleagues, neighbours, a community they're part of. When that person says a clinic was good, it reads as a recommendation. When someone with two million followers says it, it reads as an ad, because it is one and everybody knows it.

The economics compound the effect. ₹5 lakh buys one celebrity post: one hook, one script, no way to iterate. The same money runs twenty nano creators, tells you which two hooks produce enquiries, and hands you those hooks as paid creative — usually where the return actually sits.

So treat influencer spend the way we treat [performance marketing](/performance): a testing budget with a media outcome attached, not a reach purchase. Buy on cost per qualified enquiry, tracked with clean [UTM parameters](/glossary/utm-parameters) and a unique code per creator.

sections.h2: Spotting a bought audience before you pay
body: Followers cost less than the campaign does, so assume nothing. Five checks, ten minutes per creator.
numbered: **Ask for a screen recording of their insights**, scrolling live, not a screenshot. Screenshots get edited. A creator with real numbers has no reason to refuse.
**Check audience location against content language.** A Hindi-language creator with most of their audience outside India is selling followers, not reach.
**Read fifty comments.** Emoji strings and generic praise arriving in a tight burst minutes after posting is a pod or a bot farm. Real comment sections argue and go off-topic.
**Compare story views to post likes.** Story views are harder to inflate. Views far below likes is the clearest single tell.
**Look at the follower growth graph.** Organic growth is lumpy but continuous. A vertical step with no post to explain it is a purchase.

body: Most campaigns fail in the brief. Either it's a one-line WhatsApp message and the creator invents your messaging, or it's a 40-slide deck with a word-for-word script, in which case you've paid a premium for a voiceover artist.

A brief that works fits on one page: the single message the post must land; what must not be said, especially in regulated categories like health, finance and education; format and length; where the link or code goes; the disclosure label; usage rights and duration; whitelisting, if you'll run it as an ad from their handle; and a deadline with one round of feedback, not four.

Then leave the words to them. You're buying their voice and an audience you don't have. If the copy has to sound like your brand, you wanted [UGC-style production](/glossary/user-generated-content), not a creator.

sections.h2: Disclosure is not optional in India
body: ASCI's guidelines for influencer advertising require a disclosure label wherever there's a material connection between brand and poster — payment, free product, a discount code, anything of value. The Central Consumer Protection Authority's endorsement guidelines put obligations on the advertiser too, so "the creator didn't label it" isn't a position you want to defend.

The requirements are practical. The label — #ad, #sponsored, #collab — must be upfront and prominent: not buried behind "more", not lost in a wall of hashtags, visible long enough to read in video and throughout a livestream, and in the post's own language.

Brands resist this on the theory that disclosure kills performance. Audiences already assume a post is paid; the label mostly signals the creator isn't hiding it. A creator called out for an undisclosed ad costs the brand more, and for longer, than the campaign was worth.

faqs.q: What is influencer marketing in simple terms?
faqs.a: Paying someone with an audience to talk about your product to that audience. You're renting trust and attention that took them years to build. The fee scales with audience size; the persuasive power often doesn't, which is why small creators frequently outperform large ones.

faqs.q: How much do influencers charge in India?
faqs.a: Broadly, nano creators quote from a few thousand rupees a post, micro creators from around ₹15,000, macro from roughly ₹75,000, and celebrities from several lakh upwards. Category moves these more than follower count does, and usage rights or exclusivity can double the base fee.

faqs.q: Are nano influencers better than macro influencers?
faqs.a: For direct response, usually. Their audiences know them personally, and the low per-post cost lets you test many hooks instead of betting everything on one. For a launch moment where you need many people to see one thing on one day, macro reach still does something nano can't.

faqs.q: How do I know if an influencer has fake followers?
faqs.a: Ask for a live screen recording of their insights rather than a screenshot. Then check audience location against content language, read fifty comments for generic burst engagement, compare story views to post likes, and look for vertical steps in the follower graph with no post to explain them.

faqs.q: Do influencers have to disclose paid posts in India?
faqs.a: Yes. ASCI's influencer guidelines require a clear, upfront disclosure label wherever there's a material connection, including free product and discount codes. The CCPA's endorsement guidelines place obligations on advertisers too, so the brand carries risk when a creator fails to label.

faqs.q: Is influencer marketing better than SEO?
faqs.a: They do different things on different timelines. Influencer posts create demand quickly and stop working when you stop paying. SEO captures demand that already exists and compounds. Most brands eventually need both — see [SEO versus influencer marketing](/compare/seo-vs-influencer-marketing).
